Appendix A Additional Synthetic Prior Details

The synthetic prior used for pretraining was generated offline and stored as a frozen bank. Construction proceeded in two stages. First, a bank of univariate temporal base series was generated from compositional trend, seasonal, and stochastic components. Each base series was then lifted to a sampled road subgraph and modified using node-specific gains, random-walk diffusion, and graph-correlated process noise. The resulting bank contains one million multivariate series of length T=12,000T=12{,}000.

Temporal Base Generator

The univariate temporal component builds on the compositional synthetic priors introduced by ForecastPFN and subsequently adapted by LaT-PFN (Dooley et al. 2023; Verdenius et al. 2024). GAS-PFN modifies this temporal base and extends it with road-network sampling and graph-structured spatial perturbations to produce multivariate traffic processes. The precise modifications and parameter distributions are documented below.

Let ii index a univariate series and t∈{0,…,T−1}t\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\} index its stored time points. Several hyperparameters are shared by series generated together in a vectorized generator call. We denote by 𝒞\mathcal{C} the index set of series produced in one such call and state explicitly when a sampled quantity is shared within 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Unless noted otherwise, the underlying random draws are independent.

Synthetic time coordinate.

A temporal resolution is sampled once per generator call as

Uρ∼𝒰⁡(log2⁡6,log2⁡61),ρ=2Uρ−150.U_{\rho}\sim\mathcal{U}(\log_{2}6,\log_{2}61),\qquad\rho=\frac{2^{U_{\rho}}-1}{50}. (1)

The corresponding coordinate span and time coordinate are

xmax=⌈Tρ⌉,x⁡(t)=tT−1​xmax.x_{\max}=\left\lceil\frac{T}{\rho}\right\rceil,\qquad x(t)=\frac{t}{T-1}x_{\max}. (2)

The coordinate x⁡(t)x(t) is measured in nominal days for the purpose of constructing weekly, monthly, and annual seasonal phases. It does not represent a real calendar timestamp.

Trend component.

For each series i∈𝒞i\in\mathcal{C}, the raw linear slope is sampled as

λ~ilin=−0.015+0.03​Bilin+0.005​ξilin.\widetilde{\lambda}^{\mathrm{lin}}_{i}=-0.015+0.03B^{\mathrm{lin}}_{i}+0.005\xi^{\mathrm{lin}}_{i}. (3)

Here, Bilin∼Beta⁡(2,2)B^{\mathrm{lin}}_{i}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2) and ξilin∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\xi^{\mathrm{lin}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) are independent. Slopes generated in the same call are aligned to the sign of their median:

λilin=|λ~ilin|​sign⁡(mediani′∈𝒞⁡λ~i′lin).\lambda^{\mathrm{lin}}_{i}=\left|\widetilde{\lambda}^{\mathrm{lin}}_{i}\right|\operatorname{sign}\left(\operatorname{median}_{i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}}\widetilde{\lambda}^{\mathrm{lin}}_{i^{\prime}}\right). (4)

The linear offset is sampled independently for each series:

oilin∼𝒰⁡(−1,1.2).o^{\mathrm{lin}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{U}(-1,1.2). (5)

For the exponential component, let

Biexp∼Beta⁡(2,2),ξiexp∼𝒩⁡(0,1).B^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2),\qquad\xi^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). (6)

The raw exponential base is

b~iexp=\displaystyle\widetilde{b}^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i}={} 1+300log2[2−1/60000\displaystyle 1+300\log_{2}\!\Bigl[2^{-1/60000} (7)
+(21/600−2−1/60000)Bexpi+0.001ξexpi].\displaystyle+\left(2^{1/600}-2^{-1/60000}\right)B^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i}+0.001\xi^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i}\Bigr].

As with the linear slope, deviations from one are aligned to a common sign within the generator call:

biexp=1+|b~iexp−1|​sign⁡[mediani′∈𝒞⁡(b~i′exp−1)].b^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i}=1+\left|\widetilde{b}^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i}-1\right|\operatorname{sign}\left[\operatorname{median}_{i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}}\left(\widetilde{b}^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i^{\prime}}-1\right)\right]. (8)

The exponential offset and lower-bounded base are

oiexp∼𝒰⁡(−1.5,2),b¯iexp=max⁡(biexp,10−5).o^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{U}(-1.5,2),\qquad\overline{b}^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i}=\max\!\left(b^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i},10^{-5}\right). (9)

Combining the linear and exponential components gives the total trend factor

𝒯i​(t)=\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{i}(t)={} [1+λilin​(x⁡(t)−oilin​xmax)]\displaystyle\left[1+\lambda^{\mathrm{lin}}_{i}\left(x(t)-o^{\mathrm{lin}}_{i}x_{\max}\right)\right] (10)
×(b¯iexp)x⁡(t)/xmax−oiexp.\displaystyle\times\left(\overline{b}^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i}\right)^{x(t)/x_{\max}-o^{\mathrm{exp}}_{i}}.

The lower bound in Eq. (9) applies only to the base of the exponential component; the resulting trend and final temporal series are not clipped.

Seasonal component.

Let

𝒥={yr,mo,wk}\mathcal{J}=\{\mathrm{yr},\mathrm{mo},\mathrm{wk}\} (11)

index the annual, monthly, and weekly seasonal families. For a cycle length q>0q>0 and bin width p>0p>0, define

ιq,p​(x)=⌊xp⌋+1\iota_{q,p}(x)=\left\lfloor\frac{x}{p}\right\rfloor+1 (12)

and

binq,p⁡(x)={ιq,p​(x),ιq,p​(x)≤q,(ιq,p​(x)modq)+1,ιq,p​(x)>q.\operatorname{bin}_{q,p}(x)=\begin{cases}\iota_{q,p}(x),&\iota_{q,p}(x)\leq q,\\[2.84526pt] \bigl(\iota_{q,p}(x)\bmod q\bigr)+1,&\iota_{q,p}(x)>q.\end{cases} (13)

The seasonal phases are

ϕyr​(t)\displaystyle\phi_{\mathrm{yr}}(t) =bin12,30.417⁡(x⁡(t))12,\displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{bin}_{12,30.417}(x(t))}{12}, (14)
ϕmo​(t)\displaystyle\phi_{\mathrm{mo}}(t) =bin30.417,1⁡(x⁡(t))30.417,\displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{bin}_{30.417,1}(x(t))}{30.417},
ϕwk​(t)\displaystyle\phi_{\mathrm{wk}}(t) =bin7,1⁡(x⁡(t))7.\displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{bin}_{7,1}(x(t))}{7}.

For each series, the corresponding seasonal amplitudes are

ωi,yr\displaystyle\omega_{i,\mathrm{yr}} =−12+24​Bi,yr+0.15​ξi,yrsea,\displaystyle=-12+24B_{i,\mathrm{yr}}+0.15\xi^{\mathrm{sea}}_{i,\mathrm{yr}}, (15)
ωi,mo\displaystyle\omega_{i,\mathrm{mo}} =−6+12​Bi,mo+0.15​ξi,mosea,\displaystyle=-6+12B_{i,\mathrm{mo}}+0.15\xi^{\mathrm{sea}}_{i,\mathrm{mo}},
ωi,wk\displaystyle\omega_{i,\mathrm{wk}} =−3+6​Bi,wk+0.15​ξi,wksea,\displaystyle=-3+6B_{i,\mathrm{wk}}+0.15\xi^{\mathrm{sea}}_{i,\mathrm{wk}},

where

Bi,j∼Beta⁡(2,2),ξi,jsea∼𝒩⁡(0,1),j∈𝒥,B_{i,j}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2),\qquad\xi^{\mathrm{sea}}_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),\qquad j\in\mathcal{J}, (16)

with independent draws across series and seasonal families. Because Gaussian perturbations are added after the Beta-scaled draws, the displayed endpoint values are not strict support bounds.

The number of harmonics for each seasonal family is sampled independently and uniformly:

Hj​∼iid​DiscreteUniform⁡{2,3,4,5,6,7},j∈𝒥.H_{j}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{DiscreteUniform}\{2,3,4,5,6,7\},\qquad j\in\mathcal{J}. (17)

Each HjH_{j} is shared by the series in the same generator call. For series ii, family jj, and harmonic h∈{1,…,Hj}h\in\{1,\ldots,H_{j}\}, raw sine and cosine coefficients are sampled independently as

a~i​j​h∼𝒩⁡(0,h−2),c~i​j​h∼𝒩⁡(0,h−2).\widetilde{a}_{ijh}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,h^{-2}),\qquad\widetilde{c}_{ijh}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,h^{-2}). (18)

The coefficients for each seasonal family are normalized jointly over the series and harmonic dimensions of the generator call. Define

κj=[∑i∈𝒞∑h=1Hj(a~i​j​h 2+c~i​j​h 2)]1/2.\kappa_{j}=\left[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}}\sum_{h=1}^{H_{j}}\left(\widetilde{a}_{ijh}^{\,2}+\widetilde{c}_{ijh}^{\,2}\right)\right]^{1/2}. (19)

The normalized coefficients are

ai​j​h=a~i​j​hκj,ci​j​h=c~i​j​hκj.a_{ijh}=\frac{\widetilde{a}_{ijh}}{\kappa_{j}},\qquad c_{ijh}=\frac{\widetilde{c}_{ijh}}{\kappa_{j}}. (20)

The Fourier component for seasonal family jj is

Fi​j​(t)=∑h=1Hj[ai​j​h​sin⁡(2​π​h​ϕj​(t))+ci​j​h​cos⁡(2​π​h​ϕj​(t))].F_{ij}(t)=\sum_{h=1}^{H_{j}}\left[a_{ijh}\sin\!\left(2\pi h\phi_{j}(t)\right)+c_{ijh}\cos\!\left(2\pi h\phi_{j}(t)\right)\right]. (21)

The complete seasonal factor is

si​(t)=∏j∈𝒥[1+ωi,j​Fi​j​(t)].s_{i}(t)=\prod_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\left[1+\omega_{i,j}F_{ij}(t)\right]. (22)

No clipping or positivity constraint is imposed on the individual seasonal factors or their product.

Stochastic component and composition.

The Weibull shape parameter is sampled independently for each series:

ki=0.5+3​Biwei,Biwei∼Beta⁡(2,2).k_{i}=0.5+3B^{\mathrm{wei}}_{i},\qquad B^{\mathrm{wei}}_{i}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(2,2). (23)

Once per generator call, a noise-amplitude interval is selected as

(Lν,Uν)={(0,0.2),with probability ​0.4,(0.3,0.7),with probability ​0.4,(0.8,1.2),with probability ​0.2.(L_{\nu},U_{\nu})=\begin{cases}(0,0.2),&\text{with probability }0.4,\\ (0.3,0.7),&\text{with probability }0.4,\\ (0.8,1.2),&\text{with probability }0.2.\end{cases} (24)

Conditional on this shared interval, the series-level noise amplitude is sampled independently as

νi∼𝒰⁡(Lν,Uν).\nu_{i}\sim\mathcal{U}(L_{\nu},U_{\nu}). (25)

Let

Ri​(t)∼Weibull⁡(ki,1)R_{i}(t)\sim\operatorname{Weibull}(k_{i},1) (26)

denote a unit-scale Weibull realization sampled independently over series and time. Its median-rescaled form is

Wi(t)=(log2)−1/kiRi(t),W_{i}(t)=(\log 2)^{-1/k_{i}}R_{i}(t), (27)

for which median⁡[Wi​(t)]=1\operatorname{median}[W_{i}(t)]=1. The resulting multiplicative stochastic factor is

mi​(t)=1+νi​[Wi​(t)−1].m_{i}(t)=1+\nu_{i}\left[W_{i}(t)-1\right]. (28)

An overall amplitude is sampled independently for each series:

ζi∼𝒰⁡(0.5,4).\zeta_{i}\sim\mathcal{U}(0.5,4). (29)

The composition branch and additive-branch trend weight are sampled once per generator call:

χadd∼Bernoulli⁡(0.5),wadd∼𝒰⁡(0.2,0.3),\chi_{\mathrm{add}}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.5),\qquad w_{\mathrm{add}}\sim\mathcal{U}(0.2,0.3), (30)

where χadd=1\chi_{\mathrm{add}}=1 selects additive composition and χadd=0\chi_{\mathrm{add}}=0 selects multiplicative composition.

The stored univariate temporal base is

y0,i​(t)={ζi​[wadd​𝒯i​(t)+si​(t)]​𝒯i​(t)​mi​(t),χadd=1,ζi​𝒯i​(t)2​si​(t)​mi​(t),χadd=0.y_{0,i}(t)=\begin{cases}\zeta_{i}\left[w_{\mathrm{add}}\mathcal{T}_{i}(t)+s_{i}(t)\right]\mathcal{T}_{i}(t)m_{i}(t),&\chi_{\mathrm{add}}=1,\\[5.69054pt] \zeta_{i}\mathcal{T}_{i}(t)^{2}s_{i}(t)m_{i}(t),&\chi_{\mathrm{add}}=0.\end{cases} (31)

Equation (31) makes the final trend multiplication explicit: after the additive or multiplicative composition is formed, it is multiplied by 𝒯i​(t)\mathcal{T}_{i}(t) and mi​(t)m_{i}(t). The multiplicative branch therefore contains 𝒯i​(t)2\mathcal{T}_{i}(t)^{2}. No normalization, standardization, clipping, discretization, zero inflation, non-negativity transformation, or acceptance–rejection step is applied to the resulting temporal base series.

Road-Graph Bank and Subgraph Sampling

Graph-bank construction procedure.

The road-graph bank was constructed from OpenStreetMap drive networks obtained through OSMnx. It contains networks for 20 U.S. metropolitan areas: Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Houston, Los Angeles, Miami, Minneapolis, New York, Philadelphia, Phoenix, Portland, Sacramento, San Diego, San Francisco, San Jose, Seattle, and Washington, DC.

For each metropolitan area, the road topology was simplified and its largest weakly connected component was retained. Networks containing more than 512 nodes were reduced to 512 nodes by breadth-first expansion from a maximum-degree node in an undirected view of the graph.

The OpenStreetMap data accessed through OSMnx are used only to define road connectivity and direction; no traffic measurements or spatiotemporal observations from the benchmark datasets enter synthetic-prior generation. For a sampled graph with NN nodes, let 𝐀d∈{0,1}N×N\mathbf{A}_{d}\in\{0,1\}^{N\times N} denote its directed adjacency matrix. For nodes vv and v′v^{\prime},

(𝐀d)v​v′=𝕀[v→v′],(\mathbf{A}_{d})_{vv^{\prime}}=\mathbb{I}\!\left[v\rightarrow v^{\prime}\right], (32)

where 𝕀⁡[⋅]\mathbb{I}[\cdot] is the indicator function and v→v′v\rightarrow v^{\prime} denotes a directed road edge. Parallel edges between the same ordered pair are collapsed to one binary entry. The corresponding undirected adjacency is

𝐀u=𝕀[𝐀d+𝐀d⊤>0],\mathbf{A}_{u}=\mathbb{I}\!\left[\mathbf{A}_{d}+\mathbf{A}_{d}^{\top}>0\right], (33)

where the indicator is applied elementwise. Road length, geographic distance, speed, road class, geometry, coordinates, and other edge attributes are not used as adjacency or diffusion weights.

Subgraph-sampling procedure.

The multivariate bank is divided into 50 shards. Target subgraph sizes cycle through 24, 36, 48, and 60 nodes across successive shards. For each shard, one eligible metropolitan network is selected uniformly. A connected component large enough to contain the target number of nodes is selected, a root node is sampled within that component, and a connected subgraph of the target size is extracted by breadth-first expansion with randomized neighbor order. The 50 shards use seeds 42–91 for network and subgraph sampling. Metropolitan networks are sampled independently across shards, so repeated selections are allowed.

Realized graph bank.

One sampled subgraph is fixed for each shard and shared by all 20,000 multivariate series in that shard. The frozen bank used in the reported experiments therefore contains 50 fixed graph configurations: 13 with 24 nodes, 13 with 36 nodes, 12 with 48 nodes, and 12 with 60 nodes.

Graph-Structured Multivariate Process

Fix a temporal base series y0​(t)y_{0}(t) generated by Eq. (31) and a sampled graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), where VV and EE are its node and edge sets and N=|V|N=|V|. We omit the temporal-series index ii in the remainder of this section.

For r∈{u,d}r\in\{u,d\}, where uu and dd denote the undirected and directed graphs, respectively, define

𝐀~r\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{r} =𝐀r+𝐈N,\displaystyle=\mathbf{A}_{r}+\mathbf{I}_{N}, (34)
𝐃r\displaystyle\mathbf{D}_{r} =diag⁡(𝐀~r​𝟏N),\displaystyle=\operatorname{diag}\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{r}\mathbf{1}_{N}\right),
𝐏r\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{r} =𝐃r−1​𝐀~r.\displaystyle=\mathbf{D}_{r}^{-1}\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{r}.

Here, 𝐈N\mathbf{I}_{N} is the N×NN\times N identity matrix, 𝟏N\mathbf{1}_{N} is the NN-dimensional all-ones vector, and 𝟎N\mathbf{0}_{N} denotes the NN-dimensional zero vector. The sampled subgraphs used in the reported frozen bank contained no diagonal adjacency entries before 𝐈N\mathbf{I}_{N} was added, so each node receives one explicit self-loop.

Both 𝐏u\mathbf{P}_{u} and 𝐏d\mathbf{P}_{d} are row-stochastic random-walk matrices. Under the directed convention in Eq. (32), row vv of 𝐏d\mathbf{P}_{d} averages node vv with its outgoing road neighbors. For a graph signal 𝐱∈ℝN\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}, define the one-step lazy random-walk operator

𝒫r​(𝐱)=12​(𝐱+𝐏r​𝐱),r∈{u,d}.\mathcal{P}_{r}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{P}_{r}\mathbf{x}\right),\qquad r\in\{u,d\}. (35)

The graph-diffusion operator 𝒫\mathcal{P} used in the main-paper overview is the undirected operator 𝒫u\mathcal{P}_{u} used here.

The temporal base is replicated across graph nodes as

𝐲0​(t)=y0​(t)​𝟏N.\mathbf{y}_{0}(t)=y_{0}(t)\mathbf{1}_{N}. (36)

Node-specific gains are sampled once per multivariate series and remain fixed over time:

𝝃g\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\xi}_{g} ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎N,𝐈N),\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}_{N},\mathbf{I}_{N}), (37)
𝐠\displaystyle\mathbf{g} =𝟏N+σg​𝝃g,\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}_{N}+\sigma_{g}\boldsymbol{\xi}_{g},
𝐳⁡(t)\displaystyle\mathbf{z}(t) =𝐠⊙𝐲0​(t),\displaystyle=\mathbf{g}\odot\mathbf{y}_{0}(t),

where ⊙\odot denotes elementwise multiplication and σg=0.05\sigma_{g}=0.05.

The deterministic graph-propagated signal is

𝐳prop​(t)=(1−β)​𝐳​(t)+β​𝒫u​(𝐳⁡(t)),β=0.7.\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{prop}}(t)=(1-\beta)\mathbf{z}(t)+\beta\mathcal{P}_{u}\!\left(\mathbf{z}(t)\right),\qquad\beta=0.7. (38)

Equivalently,

𝐳prop​(t)=0.65​𝐳​(t)+0.35​𝐏u​𝐳​(t).\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{prop}}(t)=0.65\mathbf{z}(t)+0.35\mathbf{P}_{u}\mathbf{z}(t). (39)

Thus, deterministic propagation of the temporal signal uses only the undirected road topology. The remaining weight 1−β=0.31-\beta=0.3 is an identity contribution, not a directed-transport term.

For the process-noise component, a Gaussian vector is sampled independently at each time and independently of the node gains:

𝐧⁡(t)∼𝒩⁡(𝟎N,𝐈N).\mathbf{n}(t)\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}_{N},\mathbf{I}_{N}). (40)

The same realization is filtered through both graph operators. Following the notation in the main paper, we absorb the process-noise scale into ϵG​(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{G}(t):

ϵG​(t)\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{G}(t) =σϵ​[β​𝒫u​(𝐧⁡(t))+(1−β)​𝒫d​(𝐧⁡(t))],\displaystyle=\sigma_{\epsilon}\Big[\beta\mathcal{P}_{u}\!\left(\mathbf{n}(t)\right)+(1-\beta)\mathcal{P}_{d}\!\left(\mathbf{n}(t)\right)\Big], (41)
σϵ\displaystyle\sigma_{\epsilon} =0.02.\displaystyle=0.02.

The final multivariate signal is

𝐲⁡(t)\displaystyle\mathbf{y}(t) =𝐲0​(t)+α⁡[𝐳prop​(t)−𝐲0​(t)+ϵG​(t)],\displaystyle=\mathbf{y}_{0}(t)+\alpha\Big[\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{prop}}(t)-\mathbf{y}_{0}(t)+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{G}(t)\Big], (42)
α\displaystyle\alpha =0.05.\displaystyle=0.05.

For reference, the complete process-noise contribution after applying the outer scale α\alpha is

α​ϵG​(t)=\displaystyle\alpha\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{G}(t)={} 0.0005​𝐧​(t)+0.00035​𝐏u​𝐧​(t)\displaystyle 0.0005\mathbf{n}(t)+0.00035\mathbf{P}_{u}\mathbf{n}(t) (43)
+0.00015​𝐏d​𝐧​(t).\displaystyle+0.00015\mathbf{P}_{d}\mathbf{n}(t).

The directed adjacency enters through the graph-correlated process-noise component, whereas deterministic propagation uses the undirected road topology.

Appendix B Additional Method Details

This section provides additional details on pretraining-task sampling, context construction, tokenization, neighborhood routing, attention masking, and the training objective. The synthetic spatiotemporal prior is described separately in Appendix A.

Pretraining Task Construction

Each pretraining task begins with one multivariate realization {𝐲⁡(t)}t=0T−1\{\mathbf{y}(t)\}_{t=0}^{T-1} and its associated graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), where 𝐲⁡(t)∈ℝ|V|\mathbf{y}(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|} and T=12,000T=12{,}000. The lookback and forecast lengths are fixed to

L=H=18.L=H=18. (44)
Temporal partition.

Let

Tsplit=⌊0.8​T⌋.T_{\mathrm{split}}=\left\lfloor 0.8T\right\rfloor. (45)

Eligible context and query endpoints are

ℰctx={τ:\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ctx}}=\{\,\tau: L−1≤τ≤T−H−1,\displaystyle L-1\leq\tau\leq T-H-1, (46)
τ+H≤Tsplit},\displaystyle\tau+H\leq T_{\mathrm{split}}\,\},

and

ℰqry={τ:\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{qry}}=\{\,\tau: L−1≤τ≤T−H−1,\displaystyle L-1\leq\tau\leq T-H-1, (47)
τ−L+1≥Tsplit}.\displaystyle\tau-L+1\geq T_{\mathrm{split}}\,\}.

Every context target therefore ends at or before the temporal split, while every query lookback begins at or after it.

Context and query sampling.

The number of raw context patches is sampled as

C=⌊exp⁡(UC)⌋,UC∼𝒰⁡(log⁡64,log⁡768),C=\left\lfloor\exp(U_{C})\right\rfloor,\qquad U_{C}\sim\mathcal{U}\left(\log 64,\log 768\right), (48)

and the number of query patches is

Q∼DiscreteUniform⁡{1,…,32}.Q\sim\operatorname{DiscreteUniform}\{1,\ldots,32\}. (49)

For each context occurrence r∈{1,…,C}r\in\{1,\ldots,C\}, an endpoint τrctx\tau_{r}^{\mathrm{ctx}} is sampled uniformly from ℰctx\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ctx}} and a node vrctxv_{r}^{\mathrm{ctx}} is sampled uniformly from VV. Query occurrences are sampled analogously from ℰqry\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{qry}} and VV. Sampling is performed with replacement.

For each node vv, let

𝒞vraw={τrctx:vrctx=v}\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{raw}}_{v}=\left\{\tau_{r}^{\mathrm{ctx}}:v_{r}^{\mathrm{ctx}}=v\right\} (50)

denote its raw context-endpoint collection, and let

𝒬v={τrqry:vrqry=v}\mathcal{Q}_{v}=\left\{\tau_{r}^{\mathrm{qry}}:v_{r}^{\mathrm{qry}}=v\right\} (51)

denote its query-endpoint collection. These collections are treated as multisets during pretraining because duplicate node–endpoint draws are possible. A task need not contain every node in the stored graph. The task-local graph is restricted to the distinct nodes represented by at least one context or query occurrence.

For a node vv and endpoint τ\tau, the node-local lookback and target patches are

𝐱v,τ=[yv​(τ−L+1),…,yv​(τ)]∈ℝL,\mathbf{x}_{v,\tau}=\left[y_{v}(\tau-L+1),\ldots,y_{v}(\tau)\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{L}, (52)

and

𝐲v,τ=[yv​(τ+1),…,yv​(τ+H)]∈ℝH.\mathbf{y}_{v,\tau}=\left[y_{v}(\tau+1),\ldots,y_{v}(\tau+H)\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{H}. (53)

Overlapping windows and exact duplicate patches are permitted.

Task-level scaling.

A shared normalizer is computed from all scalar values in the sampled context lookbacks. Let μctx\mu_{\mathrm{ctx}} and mctxm_{\mathrm{ctx}} denote their mean and median, respectively, and define

sctx=max⁡{1.4826​medianr,ℓ​|xr​ℓ−mctx|,0.10}.s_{\mathrm{ctx}}=\max\left\{1.4826\,\operatorname{median}_{r,\ell}\left|x_{r\ell}-m_{\mathrm{ctx}}\right|,0.10\right\}. (54)

Every context and query lookback and target is transformed elementwise as

𝒩task​(𝐚)=clip⁡(𝐚−μctxsctx,−10,10).\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{task}}(\mathbf{a})=\operatorname{clip}\left(\frac{\mathbf{a}-\mu_{\mathrm{ctx}}}{s_{\mathrm{ctx}}},-10,10\right). (55)

No missing-value or zero-target mask is synthesized during pretraining.

Tokenization and Sequence Assembly

Let 𝐱¯v,τ\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{v,\tau} and 𝐲¯v,τ\overline{\mathbf{y}}_{v,\tau} denote the normalized lookback and target patches under the active preprocessing pipeline. During pretraining, these are obtained using Eq. (55); benchmark preprocessing is described in Appendix C.

Context and query patches are embedded by separate affine projections:

𝐞v,τctx=𝐖ctx​[𝐱¯v,τ;𝐲¯v,τ]+𝐛ctx,\mathbf{e}^{\mathrm{ctx}}_{v,\tau}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{ctx}}\left[\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{v,\tau};\overline{\mathbf{y}}_{v,\tau}\right]+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{ctx}}, (56)

and

𝐞v,τqry=𝐖qry​[𝐱¯v,τ;𝟎H]+𝐛qry,\mathbf{e}^{\mathrm{qry}}_{v,\tau}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{qry}}\left[\overline{\mathbf{x}}_{v,\tau};\mathbf{0}_{H}\right]+\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{qry}}, (57)

where

𝐖ctx,𝐖qry∈ℝd×(L+H),𝐛ctx,𝐛qry∈ℝd,\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{ctx}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{qry}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times(L+H)},\qquad\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{ctx}},\mathbf{b}_{\mathrm{qry}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, (58)

d=512d=512, and 𝟎H\mathbf{0}_{H} is the HH-dimensional zero vector. The two projections have independent parameters and contain no additional normalization, activation, or hidden layer.

Each token retains its node vv, endpoint τ\tau, and context/query role as separate metadata. These metadata are used to construct attention masks, temporal attention terms, and routed neighborhoods; they are not added to the token value. The architecture contains no node embedding, timestamp embedding, context/query type embedding, or absolute sequence-position embedding.

After context construction, let 𝒞~v\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{v} denote the retained context endpoints for node vv. The Transformer input is assembled as

𝐙(0)=[(𝐞v,τctx)v∈Vtok,τ∈𝒞~v;(𝐞v,τqry)v∈Vtok,τ∈𝒬v],\mathbf{Z}^{(0)}=\left[\left(\mathbf{e}^{\mathrm{ctx}}_{v,\tau}\right)_{v\in V_{\mathrm{tok}},\,\tau\in\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{v}};\left(\mathbf{e}^{\mathrm{qry}}_{v,\tau}\right)_{v\in V_{\mathrm{tok}},\,\tau\in\mathcal{Q}_{v}}\right], (59)

where

Vtok={v∈V:𝒞~v≠∅​or​𝒬v≠∅}.V_{\mathrm{tok}}=\left\{v\in V:\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{v}\neq\varnothing\ \text{or}\ \mathcal{Q}_{v}\neq\varnothing\right\}. (60)

All retained context occurrences precede all query occurrences. Context tokens are globally ordered by endpoint before the query block is appended. Chronology enters the model through endpoint metadata and attention constraints rather than absolute sequence position.

Context Construction

The reported checkpoints and target-dataset evaluations use different context-assembly procedures. During pretraining, a larger randomly sampled context is reduced using recent raw tokens, historical raw tokens, and attention-pooled memory tokens. During reported zero-shot evaluation, the pooling module is bypassed and each node receives K=16K=16 recent and K=16K=16 historical raw support patches.

Pretraining Context Construction

Each pretraining task initially samples between 64 and 768 context patches. The context is capped at 16 tokens per represented sensor, comprising up to eight recent raw patches, four older raw patches, and four pooled summaries of the remaining older context. Sensors with fewer sampled patches contribute fewer tokens. The resulting retained context endpoints are denoted by 𝒞~v\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{v}.

At target-dataset inference, GAS-PFN instead uses the fixed raw-support context described below.

Target-Dataset Mixed Context

Let

{τu}u=0W−1\left\{\tau_{u}\right\}_{u=0}^{W-1} (61)

denote the endpoints of all stride-one windows from the target dataset’s chronological training split, ordered by time. The recent endpoint set is

𝒞recent={τW−K,…,τW−1},K=16.\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{recent}}=\left\{\tau_{W-K},\ldots,\tau_{W-1}\right\},\qquad K=16. (62)

The same recent endpoints are used for every node, preserving temporal alignment across sensors.

Historical anchors are drawn from

ℱ={0,…,W−K−1}.\mathcal{F}=\left\{0,\ldots,W-K-1\right\}. (63)

To prefer windows with informative targets, define

ru=1|V|​H∑v∈V∑h=1H𝕀[(𝐲v,uraw)h≠0],r_{u}=\frac{1}{|V|H}\sum_{v\in V}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{I}\left[\left(\mathbf{y}^{\mathrm{raw}}_{v,u}\right)_{h}\neq 0\right], (64)

where 𝐲v,uraw\mathbf{y}^{\mathrm{raw}}_{v,u} is the original-scale target associated with training window uu, (⋅)h(\cdot)_{h} selects forecast step hh, and 𝕀⁡[⋅]\mathbb{I}[\cdot] denotes the indicator function. The preferred historical indices are

ℱ+={u∈ℱ:ru≥0.5}.\mathcal{F}^{+}=\left\{u\in\mathcal{F}:r_{u}\geq 0.5\right\}. (65)

For each node vv, eight anchors are first drawn across equal-count chronological strata of ℱ+\mathcal{F}^{+}. If fewer than eight preferred indices are available, all available preferred indices are retained and the remaining positions are filled by stratified sampling from ℱ\mathcal{F}. After removing the first group, eight additional anchors are drawn across equal-count chronological strata of the remaining historical indices.

Let

𝒞vanchor={τu:u​ is selected as an anchor for ​v}.\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{anchor}}_{v}=\left\{\tau_{u}:u\text{ is selected as an anchor for }v\right\}. (66)

Anchor selection is performed independently for each node, so historical anchors need not align across sensors. Selected anchor indices are unique within a node, although their lookback or target windows may overlap.

The retained target-domain context endpoints are

𝒞~v=𝒞recent∪𝒞vanchor,|𝒞~v|=32.\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{v}=\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{recent}}\cup\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{anchor}}_{v},\qquad\left|\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{v}\right|=32. (67)

Historical anchors retain their original training-window endpoints. The context is selected once and reused for all test queries and all three reported checkpoints. No attention-pooled memory tokens are supplied during target-dataset evaluation.

Graph-Representation Neighborhood Routing

The multi-channel branch uses a hard router that combines target-graph connectivity with content-derived representation similarity. Let 𝐀∈ℝ|Vtok|×|Vtok|\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V_{\mathrm{tok}}|\times|V_{\mathrm{tok}}|} denote the graph-score matrix restricted to VtokV_{\mathrm{tok}}. Before routing, its diagonal is set to one. The matrix is not otherwise symmetrized, binarized, or degree-normalized; its stored directionality and weights are retained.

Each graph-score row is independently min–max scaled:

A¯v​v′=Av​v′−minw∈Vtok⁡Av​wmaxw∈Vtok⁡Av​w−minw∈Vtok⁡Av​w+10−8.\overline{A}_{vv^{\prime}}=\frac{A_{vv^{\prime}}-\displaystyle\min_{w\in V_{\mathrm{tok}}}A_{vw}}{\displaystyle\max_{w\in V_{\mathrm{tok}}}A_{vw}-\displaystyle\min_{w\in V_{\mathrm{tok}}}A_{vw}+10^{-8}}. (68)
Content-derived representations.

A fixed, seed-initialized MLP ψω0:ℝd→ℝd\psi_{\omega_{0}}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} is applied to the learned patch-token embeddings:

ψω0​(𝐳)\displaystyle\psi_{\omega_{0}}(\mathbf{z}) =𝐖2​Drop0.1​[GELU⁡(𝐖1​LN⁡(𝐳)+𝐛1)]+𝐛2.\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}_{2}\operatorname{Drop}_{0.1}\!\left[\operatorname{GELU}\!\left(\mathbf{W}_{1}\operatorname{LN}(\mathbf{z})+\mathbf{b}_{1}\right)\right]+\mathbf{b}_{2}. (69)

where LN\operatorname{LN} denotes layer normalization, 𝐖1,𝐖2∈ℝd×d\mathbf{W}_{1},\mathbf{W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, and 𝐛1,𝐛2∈ℝd\mathbf{b}_{1},\mathbf{b}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Dropout is disabled during evaluation.

For each represented node, define the multiset of its context and query endpoints as

𝒯v=𝒞~v⊎𝒬v,\mathcal{T}_{v}=\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{v}\uplus\mathcal{Q}_{v}, (70)

where ⊎\uplus denotes multiset union. Its encoded summary is

𝐡v=1|𝒯v|​∑τ∈𝒯vψω0​(𝐙v,τ(0)).\mathbf{h}_{v}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{v}|}\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}_{v}}\psi_{\omega_{0}}\left(\mathbf{Z}^{(0)}_{v,\tau}\right). (71)

When multiple token occurrences share the same (v,τ)(v,\tau) metadata, each occurrence contributes separately to the sum.

The summary is normalized as

𝐡^v=𝐡vmax⁡(‖𝐡v‖2,10−12),\widehat{\mathbf{h}}_{v}=\frac{\mathbf{h}_{v}}{\max\left(\|\mathbf{h}_{v}\|_{2},10^{-12}\right)}, (72)

and semantic similarity is

Sv​v′sem=𝐡^v⊤​𝐡^v′.S^{\mathrm{sem}}_{vv^{\prime}}=\widehat{\mathbf{h}}_{v}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{h}}_{v^{\prime}}. (73)

The hybrid routing score is

Sv​v′hyb=(1−η)​A¯v​v′+η​Sv​v′sem,η=0.4.S^{\mathrm{hyb}}_{vv^{\prime}}=(1-\eta)\overline{A}_{vv^{\prime}}+\eta S^{\mathrm{sem}}_{vv^{\prime}},\qquad\eta=0.4. (74)

For each node vv, the routed neighborhood is

𝒩v=TopKv′⁡(Sv​v′hyb,kv),kv=min⁡(7,|Vtok|).\mathcal{N}_{v}=\operatorname{TopK}_{v^{\prime}}\left(S^{\mathrm{hyb}}_{vv^{\prime}},k_{v}\right),\qquad k_{v}=\min\left(7,|V_{\mathrm{tok}}|\right). (75)

Selection is performed independently by row and is not symmetrized. Self-membership is determined by the score rather than imposed separately.

The hard TopK indices are converted directly into a Boolean attention mask; the continuous routing scores are not passed to the Transformer. The routing path therefore provides no forecasting-loss gradient to ψω0\psi_{\omega_{0}} or to its inputs, and ω0\omega_{0} remains at its seed-specific initialization. The patch-token embeddings supplied to the router are nevertheless learned through the ordinary forecasting path, so the resulting neighborhoods remain content-dependent and may change during pretraining. This construction avoids requiring a continuous relaxation or surrogate-gradient estimator for discrete neighborhood selection.

Neighborhoods are recomputed once for each branch forward from the current token sequence. The resulting Boolean neighborhood mask is shared across all Transformer layers.

Exact Attention Constraints

A token is identified by its node and endpoint pair (v,τ)(v,\tau) together with its position in the token multiset. Duplicate occurrences sharing the same (v,τ)(v,\tau) metadata obey the same attention conditions but remain separate sequence elements. Context and query endpoint collections are disjoint in the executed pretraining and evaluation protocols.

Let

𝒜(v,τ),(v′,τ′)(b)∈{0,1}\mathcal{A}^{(b)}_{(v,\tau),(v^{\prime},\tau^{\prime})}\in\{0,1\} (76)

indicate whether token (v,τ)(v,\tau) may attend to key/value token (v′,τ′)(v^{\prime},\tau^{\prime}) in branch b∈{self,multi}b\in\{\mathrm{self},\mathrm{multi}\}.

Self branch.

The self-branch mask is

𝒜(v,τ),(v′,τ′)(self)=𝕀[v=v′]𝕀[τ′∈𝒞~v′]𝕀[τ′≤τ].\mathcal{A}^{(\mathrm{self})}_{(v,\tau),(v^{\prime},\tau^{\prime})}=\mathbb{I}[v=v^{\prime}]\,\mathbb{I}\left[\tau^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{v^{\prime}}\right]\,\mathbb{I}[\tau^{\prime}\leq\tau]. (77)

Both context and query tokens therefore attend only to causal context from the same node. Context-to-query and query-to-query attention are disabled, including query-token self-attention.

Multi-channel branch.

For the reported target-dataset evaluation,

𝒜(multi)(v,τ),(v′,τ′)=𝕀[v′∈𝒩v]\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{(\mathrm{multi})}_{(v,\tau),(v^{\prime},\tau^{\prime})}=\mathbb{I}\left[v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}_{v}\right] (78)
×{𝕀[τ′≤τ],τ′∈𝒞~v′,𝕀[τ∈𝒬v]𝕀[τ′=τ],τ′∈𝒬v′.\displaystyle\times\begin{cases}\mathbb{I}[\tau^{\prime}\leq\tau],&\tau^{\prime}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{v^{\prime}},\\[2.84526pt] \mathbb{I}\left[\tau\in\mathcal{Q}_{v}\right]\mathbb{I}[\tau^{\prime}=\tau],&\tau^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Q}_{v^{\prime}}.\end{cases}

Context-to-query attention remains blocked. Query-to-query attention is permitted only among selected nodes at the same forecast origin. Here, “same forecast time” means equality of query-window endpoints; one query token predicts all HH future steps.

During checkpoint pretraining, the query-key case instead uses

𝕀[τ∈𝒬v]𝕀[τ′≤τ],τ′∈𝒬v′,\mathbb{I}\left[\tau\in\mathcal{Q}_{v}\right]\mathbb{I}[\tau^{\prime}\leq\tau],\qquad\tau^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Q}_{v^{\prime}}, (79)

allowing a query token to attend to same-time and earlier query tokens inside its selected neighborhood. The self branch uses Eq. (77) during both pretraining and evaluation.

Attention logits.

At a given Transformer layer and attention head hh, let 𝐪v,τ(b,h)\mathbf{q}^{(b,h)}_{v,\tau} and 𝐤v′,τ′(b,h)\mathbf{k}^{(b,h)}_{v^{\prime},\tau^{\prime}} denote the query and key vectors for tokens (v,τ)(v,\tau) and (v′,τ′)(v^{\prime},\tau^{\prime}). The layer index is omitted for clarity. With hidden dimension d=512d=512 and eight heads, the head dimension is

dh=64.d_{h}=64. (80)

The unmasked attention score is

ℓ~(v,τ),(v′,τ′)(b,h)\displaystyle\widetilde{\ell}^{(b,h)}_{(v,\tau),(v^{\prime},\tau^{\prime})} =(𝐪v,τ(b,h))⊤​𝐤v′,τ′(b,h)dh\displaystyle=\frac{\left(\mathbf{q}^{(b,h)}_{v,\tau}\right)^{\top}\mathbf{k}^{(b,h)}_{v^{\prime},\tau^{\prime}}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}} (81)
−γh​max⁡(τ−τ′,0)\displaystyle-\gamma_{h}\max(\tau-\tau^{\prime},0)
+bsame,h(b)𝕀[v=v′].\displaystyle+b_{\mathrm{same},h}^{(b)}\mathbb{I}[v=v^{\prime}].

The attention mask is then applied as

ℓ(v,τ),(v′,τ′)(b,h)={ℓ~(v,τ),(v′,τ′)(b,h),𝒜(v,τ),(v′,τ′)(b)=1,−∞,otherwise.\ell^{(b,h)}_{(v,\tau),(v^{\prime},\tau^{\prime})}=\begin{cases}\widetilde{\ell}^{(b,h)}_{(v,\tau),(v^{\prime},\tau^{\prime})},&\mathcal{A}^{(b)}_{(v,\tau),(v^{\prime},\tau^{\prime})}=1,\\ -\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (82)

Each head learns its own temporal-distance coefficient γh\gamma_{h}, initialized to

γh=0.01.\gamma_{h}=0.01. (83)

The coefficients are shared across the two branches and all Transformer layers. The self-channel coefficient bsame,h(b)b_{\mathrm{same},h}^{(b)} is learned separately for each head and branch and is shared across layers. In the self branch, the self-channel term is constant over every visible key and therefore cancels under the softmax. In the multi-channel branch, it distinguishes same-node from neighboring-node interactions.

The two branches otherwise use the same patch projections, Transformer backbone, query/key/value projections, layer normalizations, and feed-forward parameters.

Fusion and Pretraining Objective

For a query token (v,τ)(v,\tau) with τ∈𝒬v\tau\in\mathcal{Q}_{v}, let

𝐮v,τself,𝐮v,τmulti∈ℝd\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{self}}_{v,\tau},\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{multi}}_{v,\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} (84)

denote the two retained backbone representations. A scalar gate is computed as

gv,τ=σ⁡(𝐰g⊤​[𝐮v,τself;𝐮v,τmulti]+bg),g_{v,\tau}=\sigma\left(\mathbf{w}_{g}^{\top}\left[\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{self}}_{v,\tau};\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{multi}}_{v,\tau}\right]+b_{g}\right), (85)

where 𝐰g∈ℝ2​d\mathbf{w}_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}, bg∈ℝb_{g}\in\mathbb{R}, and σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function. There is one scalar gate per query token, broadcast across all latent features.

The fused representation is

𝐮v,τmix=(1−gv,τ)​𝐮v,τself+gv,τ​𝐮v,τmulti.\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{mix}}_{v,\tau}=\left(1-g_{v,\tau}\right)\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{self}}_{v,\tau}+g_{v,\tau}\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{multi}}_{v,\tau}. (86)

Larger gate values therefore assign greater weight to the multi-channel representation.

A shared affine prediction head hθ:ℝd→ℝHh_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{H} produces

𝐲^v,τself\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\mathrm{self}}_{v,\tau} =hθ​(𝐮v,τself),\displaystyle=h_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{self}}_{v,\tau}\right), (87)
𝐲^v,τmulti\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\mathrm{multi}}_{v,\tau} =hθ​(𝐮v,τmulti),\displaystyle=h_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{multi}}_{v,\tau}\right),
𝐲^v,τmix\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\mathrm{mix}}_{v,\tau} =hθ​(𝐮v,τmix).\displaystyle=h_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{mix}}_{v,\tau}\right).

Let

𝒬=⨄v∈Vtok{(v,τ):τ∈𝒬v}\mathcal{Q}=\biguplus_{v\in V_{\mathrm{tok}}}\left\{(v,\tau):\tau\in\mathcal{Q}_{v}\right\} (88)

denote the multiset of query-token occurrences, so that |𝒬|=Q|\mathcal{Q}|=Q. For b∈{self,multi,mix}b\in\{\mathrm{self},\mathrm{multi},\mathrm{mix}\}, the forecast loss is

ℒb=1Q​H​∑(v,τ)∈𝒬‖𝐲^v,τb−𝐲¯v,τ‖22.\mathcal{L}_{b}=\frac{1}{QH}\sum_{(v,\tau)\in\mathcal{Q}}\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{b}_{v,\tau}-\overline{\mathbf{y}}_{v,\tau}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (89)

No missing-value or zero-target mask is applied during synthetic pretraining.

For numerical stability, define

gv,τϵ=min⁡(1−ϵ,max⁡(ϵ,gv,τ)),ϵ=10−6.g_{v,\tau}^{\epsilon}=\min\left(1-\epsilon,\max(\epsilon,g_{v,\tau})\right),\qquad\epsilon=10^{-6}. (90)

The mean binary gate entropy is

ℋgate=−1Q∑(v,τ)∈𝒬[\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{gate}}=-\frac{1}{Q}\sum_{(v,\tau)\in\mathcal{Q}}\Big[ gv,τϵ​log⁡gv,τϵ\displaystyle g_{v,\tau}^{\epsilon}\log g_{v,\tau}^{\epsilon} (91)
+(1−gv,τϵ)log(1−gv,τϵ)].\displaystyle+\left(1-g_{v,\tau}^{\epsilon}\right)\log\left(1-g_{v,\tau}^{\epsilon}\right)\Big].

The pretraining objective is

ℒ=ℒmix+0.3​ℒself+0.3​ℒmulti−0.03​ℋgate.\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mix}}+0.3\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{self}}+0.3\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{multi}}-0.03\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{gate}}. (92)

The auxiliary losses keep both branches individually predictive, while the negative entropy term discourages premature gate saturation. At inference time, only 𝐲^v,τmix\widehat{\mathbf{y}}^{\mathrm{mix}}_{v,\tau} is returned.

Appendix C Additional Experimental Details

Datasets, Splits, and Preprocessing

We evaluate on METR-LA and PEMS-BAY (Li et al. 2018) and on PEMS03, PEMS04, PEMS07, and PEMS08 (Chen et al. 2001; Guo et al. 2019). All series are treated as having nominal five-minute resolution. The executed preprocessing retains every loaded sensor and time point and performs no interpolation, resampling, deduplication, gap filling, or missing-value imputation. METR-LA and PEMS-BAY use all non-timestamp columns from their CSV files. For PEMS03, PEMS04, and PEMS08, preprocessing extracts feature index zero from the public time-by-sensor-by-feature tensors and stores the resulting time-by-sensor matrices. For PEMS07, the tensor representation is retained, and feature index zero is selected during evaluation. Calendar and timestamp features are not supplied to GAS-PFN.

Chronological splits.

For a dataset δ\delta containing TδT_{\delta} time points, the split sizes are

Tδtr=⌊0.7​Tδ⌋,Tδte=⌊0.2​Tδ⌋,T_{\delta}^{\mathrm{tr}}=\left\lfloor 0.7T_{\delta}\right\rfloor,\qquad T_{\delta}^{\mathrm{te}}=\left\lfloor 0.2T_{\delta}\right\rfloor, (93)

and

Tδval=Tδ−Tδtr−Tδte.T_{\delta}^{\mathrm{val}}=T_{\delta}-T_{\delta}^{\mathrm{tr}}-T_{\delta}^{\mathrm{te}}. (94)

The intervals are contiguous and ordered as training, validation, and test. Sliding windows are constructed separately for each split. Validation and test targets remain entirely within their respective intervals, while the first lookback in each of those intervals uses the final 18 observations immediately preceding it.

All benchmark windows use L=18L=18, H=18H=18, and stride one. Reported horizons h∈{6,12,18}h\in\{6,12,18\} are cumulative: each result aggregates forecast leads 1,…,h1,\ldots,h rather than only lead hh.

Normalization.

Let VδV_{\delta} denote the sensor set of dataset δ\delta. For each v∈Vδv\in V_{\delta}, GAS-PFN fits a separate standardizer from the training rows:

μv(δ)=1Tδtr​∑t=0Tδtr−1yv(δ)​(t),\mu_{v}^{(\delta)}=\frac{1}{T_{\delta}^{\mathrm{tr}}}\sum_{t=0}^{T_{\delta}^{\mathrm{tr}}-1}y_{v}^{(\delta)}(t), (95)
(σv(δ))2=1Tδtr​∑t=0Tδtr−1(yv(δ)​(t)−μv(δ))2,\left(\sigma_{v}^{(\delta)}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{T_{\delta}^{\mathrm{tr}}}\sum_{t=0}^{T_{\delta}^{\mathrm{tr}}-1}\left(y_{v}^{(\delta)}(t)-\mu_{v}^{(\delta)}\right)^{2}, (96)

and

y~v(δ)​(t)=yv(δ)​(t)−μv(δ)σv(δ).\widetilde{y}_{v}^{(\delta)}(t)=\frac{y_{v}^{(\delta)}(t)-\mu_{v}^{(\delta)}}{\sigma_{v}^{(\delta)}}. (97)

The same sensor-specific transformation is applied to training supports and test queries. Predictions and targets are inverse-transformed before metric computation. The synthetic task-level robust scaling in Eq. (55) is not applied to benchmark data, and no output clipping is performed.

Dataset graph inputs.

GAS-PFN consumes the stored adjacency matrix associated with each benchmark. Its diagonal is set to one before neighborhood routing; the matrix is not otherwise symmetrized, binarized, thresholded, or degree-normalized.

The METR-LA and PEMS-BAY matrices are weighted and numerically asymmetric. PEMS03, PEMS04, and PEMS08 use symmetric binary connectivity; available edge attributes beyond connectivity are not used. For PEMS07, an undirected edge with positive recorded cost cost⁡(v,v′)\operatorname{cost}(v,v^{\prime}) is assigned

Av​v′=exp⁡(−cost⁡(v,v′)σcost),A_{vv^{\prime}}=\exp\left(-\frac{\operatorname{cost}(v,v^{\prime})}{\sigma_{\mathrm{cost}}}\right), (98)

where σcost\sigma_{\mathrm{cost}} is the standard deviation of the retained positive edge costs. Parallel entries retain their maximum weight, and no threshold is applied. These stored graph matrices are distinct from the row-scaled graph scores in Eq. (68).

Evaluation Metrics

Let WδteW_{\delta}^{\mathrm{te}} denote the number of test windows for dataset δ\delta. Let y^u,s,v(δ)\widehat{y}^{(\delta)}_{u,s,v} and yu,s,v(δ)y^{(\delta)}_{u,s,v} denote the original-scale prediction and ground truth for test window u∈{1,…,Wδte}u\in\{1,\ldots,W_{\delta}^{\mathrm{te}}\}, forecast lead s∈{1,…,H}s\in\{1,\ldots,H\}, and sensor v∈Vδv\in V_{\delta}.

For cumulative horizon hh, define

Ωδ​(h)={(u,s,v):1≤u≤Wδte,1≤s≤h,v∈Vδ,yu,s,v(δ)≠0}.\Omega_{\delta}(h)=\left\{(u,s,v):\begin{array}[]{l}1\leq u\leq W_{\delta}^{\mathrm{te}},\\ 1\leq s\leq h,\\ v\in V_{\delta},\\ y^{(\delta)}_{u,s,v}\neq 0\end{array}\right\}. (99)

The reported metrics are

MAEδ⁡(h)=1|Ωδ​(h)|​∑(u,s,v)∈Ωδ​(h)|y^u,s,v(δ)−yu,s,v(δ)|,\operatorname{MAE}_{\delta}(h)=\frac{1}{|\Omega_{\delta}(h)|}\sum_{(u,s,v)\in\Omega_{\delta}(h)}\left|\widehat{y}^{(\delta)}_{u,s,v}-y^{(\delta)}_{u,s,v}\right|, (100)

and

MSEδ⁡(h)=1|Ωδ​(h)|​∑(u,s,v)∈Ωδ​(h)(y^u,s,v(δ)−yu,s,v(δ))2.\operatorname{MSE}_{\delta}(h)=\frac{1}{|\Omega_{\delta}(h)|}\sum_{(u,s,v)\in\Omega_{\delta}(h)}\left(\widehat{y}^{(\delta)}_{u,s,v}-y^{(\delta)}_{u,s,v}\right)^{2}. (101)

The zero comparison is exact and is applied to raw ground truth after inverse transformation. For each dataset, MAE and MSE are computed by pooling errors across all valid test windows, forecast steps 1,…,h1,\ldots,h, and sensors. Cross-dataset averages are unweighted arithmetic means of the six dataset-level metrics.

Zero masking in Eqs. (100) and (101) applies to benchmark evaluation. GAS-PFN’s synthetic pretraining objective does not use a benchmark zero-value mask.

GAS-PFN Configuration and Evaluation

Hyperparameters governing synthetic-prior generation are reported in Appendix A. Table 2 summarizes the architecture, optimization, and target-evaluation settings.

The three primary GAS-PFN checkpoints are independently pretrained with seeds 42, 43, and 44. Each checkpoint is the terminal state after one million optimizer steps. The frozen synthetic bank is shared across runs, while task sampling and optimization are independently seeded.

Target-domain context.

For each sensor vv, the main zero-shot evaluation uses the retained endpoint set 𝒞~v\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{v} defined in Eq. (67): 16 aligned recent supports and 16 sensor-specific historical anchors. The context is reconstructed identically for each checkpoint and cached for every test query. No attention-pooled memory tokens are used during benchmark evaluation.

Full-channel and PEMS07 inference.

METR-LA, PEMS-BAY, PEMS03, PEMS04, and PEMS08 are evaluated with all sensors present in each forward pass. PEMS07 uses memory-bounded channel-cohort inference, while the other five datasets use full-channel inference. For the channel cohort strategy, target sensors are grouped in sets of at most 50, and each group’s active context pool contains the union of the targets’ selected one-hop channel neighborhoods. The groups are assigned via a greedy algorithm designed to minimize repeated processing of the same channels for context. Every active sensor retains all 32 raw context patches.

This fallback preserves the complete selected context and planned context neighborhood of each target sensor. Query tokens are retained only for the cohort’s target sensors, and representations and routing are recomputed within the reduced token universe. The reported PEMS07 results therefore use cohort inference; the other five datasets use full-channel inference.

Checkpoint aggregation.

Let ara_{r} denote a metric obtained from checkpoint seed r∈{42,43,44}r\in\{42,43,44\}. The primary GAS-PFN table reports

a¯\displaystyle\overline{a} =13​∑r∈{42,43,44}ar,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{r\in\{42,43,44\}}a_{r}, (102)
σpop\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathrm{pop}} =[13​∑r∈{42,43,44}(ar−a¯)2]1/2.\displaystyle=\left[\frac{1}{3}\sum_{r\in\{42,43,44\}}\left(a_{r}-\overline{a}\right)^{2}\right]^{1/2}.

Zero-Shot Baseline Configuration

Chronos-2 (Ansari et al. 2025), TimesFM-2.5 (Das et al. 2024), Moirai-2 (Liu et al. 2025), Lag-Llama (Rasul et al. 2024), and TimePFN (Taga et al. 2025) are each evaluated under a recent-only and a history-augmented context regime. Except for model-specific input requirements described below, the recent-only regime uses the 18 observations immediately preceding each forecast origin. The history-augmented regime concatenates a contiguous prefix from the end of the 70% training split with the same 18 recent observations. The training prefix and recent window are disjoint.

For each baseline and dataset, both regimes are rescored using Eqs. (100) and (101). We report the regime with lower cumulative 18-step test MAE and use that single regime for every reported horizon and both metrics. The lower-MAE regime is selected once per baseline and dataset and is then used for every reported horizon and both metrics. GAS-PFN uses one fixed 32-patch support configuration.

Chronos-2 is evaluated through its multivariate data-frame interface without exogenous covariates. TimesFM-2.5 is applied independently to each sensor with its native input normalization and positive-output configuration. Moirai-2 is also applied independently by sensor, without static or dynamic covariates, and its median quantile is used as the point forecast. TimePFN is evaluated as a multivariate model over contiguous sensor blocks of at most 161 channels, with predictions restored to the original sensor order. All external prediction arrays are inverse-transformed by their corresponding wrappers and rescored using the common raw-scale metric implementation.

The external pretrained checkpoints use deterministic inference paths and are therefore reported as single values. Chronos-2, TimesFM-2.5, and Moirai-2 use their 0.50.5-quantile forecasts, Lag-Llama uses its analytic predictive mean, and TimePFN uses its direct point output; repeated executions produced byte-identical predictions.

Lag-Llama context handling.

Lag-Llama constructs its inputs using a fixed set of lagged values. Accordingly, we preserve the released model’s native lag-feature construction by providing the additional historical buffer required to instantiate those lags. Its recent-only and history-augmented configurations therefore consume 1,110 and 1,124 raw observations, respectively, even though their designated model-context lengths are 18 and 32 and the contiguous recent window remains 18 observations. This preserves the released model’s native lag-feature construction without modifying its architecture.

Additional Comparison Protocols

TimePFN fine-tuning.

The TimePFN fine-tuning comparison uses labeled-window budgets of 32 and 64 on METR-LA, PEMS-BAY, PEMS03, PEMS04, and PEMS08; PEMS07 is excluded because the registered fine-tuning configuration exceeded available GPU memory. Budgets are nested, and the same sampled window indices are shared across the two TimePFN context variants for each seed.

All TimePFN parameters are updated using AdamW with learning rate 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, weight decay 0.010.01, batch size 16, and at most eight epochs. The learning rate is halved after each epoch, early-stopping patience is three epochs, and checkpoint selection uses validation performance. Training and validation minimize original-scale, exact-zero-masked MAE. Results are aggregated over seeds 42, 43, and 44.

SCPT selected-road evaluation.

The cross-road experiment uses SCPT (Prabowo et al. 2024) with a 12-step lookback and an 18-step output. For each dataset, the fraction of roads available for SCPT training ranges from 10% to 80%; 10% of roads are reserved for validation, and the remaining roads form the unseen test set. Seeds 42, 43, and 44 define independent road permutations. Each GAS-PFN result is paired with the checkpoint having the same seed, while SCPT is trained separately for that road partition.

SCPT retains its native preprocessing, which computes one scalar mean and standard deviation over the complete time-by-road matrix before the temporal and road splits. GAS-PFN instead uses the train-only sensor-specific scaling in Eqs. (95)– (97). For the final comparison, both methods are inverse-transformed, aligned to the same raw target tensor, and rescored using the identical exact-zero mask.

The selected-road results report the arithmetic mean and sample standard deviation over the three paired model and road-partition seeds. This variation therefore includes both independently pretrained GAS-PFN checkpoints and different supervised-road partitions.

Appendix D Additional Benchmark Results

Additional Zero-shot Results

Table 4 reports both evaluated context regimes for every external baseline across all datasets and forecast horizons. “Recent 18” uses a contiguous recent window of 18 observations, while “Recent + prefix” additionally supplies a contiguous tail from the training split. The Total column reports raw temporal input per channel. For Lag-Llama, marked by †\dagger, this total also includes the longer raw-history buffer required by its native lag features, as detailed in Appendix C. GAS-PFN’s total counts 18 recent values together with 32 support patches of 36 scalar values each, yielding 1,170 scalar input slots.

These expanded results reinforce the main-paper observation that more contiguous history is not uniformly beneficial: the effect of adding a training-tail prefix varies substantially across models and datasets. GAS-PFN instead uses one fixed graph-aware mixed-context construction, supporting the claim that the organization and use of historical context matter in addition to its raw quantity.

Computing infrastructure.

All experiments were run as single-GPU jobs on a server equipped with eight NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs, AMD EPYC 7742 processors, and approximately 1.97 TiB of system memory. The server ran Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS. GAS-PFN training and evaluation used CPython 3.12.3 and PyTorch 2.6.0+cu124 with CUDA 12.4.

TimePFN Fine-Tuning Comparison

Table 5 compares zero-shot GAS-PFN with TimePFN after target-specific fine-tuning using 32 or 64 labeled patches. For TimePFN, “Recent 18” uses only the 18 observations immediately preceding each forecast origin, while “Recent + prefix” also supplies a contiguous tail from the training split. GAS-PFN instead uses its fixed mixed-context configuration and performs no target-specific parameter updates. Across the five evaluated datasets, GAS-PFN achieves the best mean result in 27 of the 30 dataset–horizon–metric comparisons. Fine-tuning TimePFN with 64 patches narrows the gap and yields the best 90-minute MSE on PEMS03, PEMS04, and PEMS08, but does not otherwise surpass GAS-PFN. These results reinforce that the graph-aware prior and in-context architecture remain competitive even against limited target-domain parameter adaptation.

Full SCPT Comparison

Table 6 expands the main-paper cross-road comparison by reporting complete MAE and MSE results at the cumulative 30-, 60-, and 90-minute horizons. SCPT12 is trained separately for each road split using the full historical record from the indicated fraction of roads, with 10% reserved for validation and the remaining roads held out for testing. GAS-PFN instead performs zero-shot inference without target-specific parameter updates. The 60-minute results reproduce the main-paper finding that GAS-PFN is strongest when supervised road coverage is limited: it outperforms SCPT12 on all six datasets at the 10% budget and on five of six datasets at both 20% and 30%. The additional horizons show the same broad pattern, while SCPT12 generally becomes more competitive as its access to supervised roads increases. Full preprocessing and split details are provided in Appendix C.

Appendix E Ablation Tests

Table 7 presents targeted frozen-checkpoint ablations of three components: dual-branch fusion, mixed-context support, and hybrid neighborhood routing. Across the resulting 36 dataset–horizon–metric settings, the full learned mixture achieves the best mean in 23 cases and ranks among the top two in 35. It outperforms both individual experts in 34 settings, while either learned or fixed equal fusion is best in 32, supporting the use of complementary self-channel and multi-channel representations. Removing the historical supports degrades performance in all 36 settings, indicating that the trained model makes effective use of its mixed-context memory. The hybrid router also outperforms graph-only routing in 33 settings, although these gains are generally smaller and remain dataset-dependent. Because these variants use frozen checkpoints, they isolate the inference-time contribution of each component.
